conventional_description: Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when the median nerve, which runs from the forearm into the hand, becomes compressed as it passes through the narrow carpal tunnel at the wrist. This compression typically causes numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index, middle, and thumb side of the ring finger. Symptoms often flare at night, and over time the hand may feel weak or clumsy, causing people to drop objects. Diagnosis is usually based on physical exam maneuvers like Tinel's sign or Phalen's test, and may be confirmed with nerve conduction studies.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment begins with wrist splinting, especially at night, and activity modification to reduce repetitive strain. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can help with pain and inflammation. If these measures fail, corticosteroid injections into the carpal tunnel may provide temporary relief. For persistent or severe cases, carpal tunnel release surgery is performed to cut the ligament pressing on the nerve, which is generally effective but involves a recovery period.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views the wrist as a narrow passageway where Qi and Blood must flow freely to nourish the hand and fingers. Several major meridians - including the Pericardium, Triple Burner, Heart, Lung, and Large Intestine channels - all travel through this tight space. When flow is blocked by stagnation, cold, dampness, heat, or phlegm, the median nerve (and the channels themselves) become compressed, producing the classic numbness, tingling, and pain. This is why TCM calls the condition a “Bi syndrome” or painful obstruction.
Excess patterns are the most common. Repetitive hand motions like typing or gripping cause Qi and Blood to stagnate locally, creating swelling and stabbing pain. When cold and dampness invade - often from exposure to cold environments or damp weather - the tissues tighten and fluids stagnate, making symptoms worse with cold and better with warmth.
In some cases, heat and dampness combine from local inflammation, causing redness and a burning sensation. Over time, untreated stagnation can thicken into Phlegm, a sticky obstruction that makes the wrist feel heavy, swollen, and dull.
Deficiency patterns develop when the body lacks the resources to nourish the wrist. Chronic fatigue, poor diet, or prolonged illness can deplete Qi and Blood, leading to weak, numb hands that tire easily.
Aging or overwork may consume Kidney and Liver Yin, the deep moisture that lubricates tendons and joints. Without this nourishment, the wrist becomes dry, tight, and prone to discomfort even with ordinary use, often accompanied by a warm or burning feeling at night.
Because the same Western diagnosis can arise from such different root imbalances, TCM doesn’t treat carpal tunnel syndrome with a one-size-fits-all approach. Instead, a practitioner carefully differentiates the pattern based on the nature of the pain, what makes it better or worse, and the tongue and pulse. This allows treatment to target the exact mechanism driving your symptoms, rather than just numbing the pain.
classical_quote: 「风、寒、湿三气杂至，合而为痹也。」
classical_translation: "When wind, cold, and dampness combine, they cause Bi syndrome. This classic statement explains the external pathogenic factors that can lodge in the carpal tunnel, creating painful obstruction."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen  ,  Chapter 43: Discussion on Bi Syndrome 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first asks about the nature of your discomfort - is it sharp, dull, burning, or heavy? They also want to know what makes it worse: repetitive activity, cold weather, or maybe rest. Your answers immediately steer the diagnosis toward one pattern or another.
If the pain is stabbing and tingling, and it flares up after prolonged typing or gripping, Qi and Blood Stagnation is likely. The tongue may appear purplish and the pulse feels wiry or choppy, confirming that the local flow has become stuck.
When symptoms worsen markedly in cold, damp weather and the wrist feels stiff and cold to the touch, Wind-Cold-Damp obstruction is the picture. The tongue coating is often white and thick, and the pulse feels tight or slow, reflecting the presence of pathogenic cold and dampness.
If your wrist and hand feel heavy, swollen, and somewhat numb - almost like wearing a thick glove - Phlegm obstructing the channels may be the cause. The tongue coating is usually greasy and the pulse slippery, pointing to a thick, sticky obstruction rather than simple stagnation.
Redness, warmth, and a burning ache suggest Damp-Heat has settled in the carpal tunnel. This pattern is more acute and inflammatory, often with a yellow greasy tongue coating and a rapid, slippery pulse. The practitioner would ask about activities that generate heat and friction.
Long-standing numbness accompanied by overall fatigue, a pale complexion, and weak grip strength points to Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is thin and weak - signs that the body lacks the resources to nourish and repair the wrist.
In a slow, chronic case with dry, stiff tendons and perhaps night sweats or a low back ache, underlying Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency may be involved. The tongue is often red with little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid, revealing a deeper constitutional weakness that fails to moisten the sinews.

patterns.symptoms: ["Stabbing, fixed pain in the wrist and hand", "Pain worsens with pressure or repetitive use", "Tingling and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers", "Dark purple tongue with stasis spots", "Wiry and choppy pulse"]
patterns.worse_with: Repetitive hand motions, Cold weather or cold water, Emotional stress, Prolonged immobility, Greasy, heavy foods
patterns.better_with: Warm compress on wrist, Gentle wrist stretches, Breaks from repetitive tasks, Warming foods like ginger, Moderate exercise to move Qi
patterns.why_this_happens: Repetitive hand motions and overuse cause Qi and Blood to stagnate in the wrist's narrow carpal tunnel. This local stagnation creates swelling and pressure on the median nerve, leading to the characteristic stabbing pain, tingling, and numbness. The pain is often worse at night or with use, and feels fixed and sharp.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, often with distended sublingual veins. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood stagnation in the wrist is like a traffic jam. Movement and warmth help to 'move' the stagnation, easing pressure on the nerve. Cold and immobility cause further constriction, making the pain worse. Emotional stress tightens the Liver Qi, which can exacerbate the stagnation, so calming the mind and reducing repetitive strain are key.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Take frequent breaks from repetitive hand tasks and stretch your wrists gently. Include warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, and dark leafy greens. Avoid cold, raw foods that can constrict circulation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Wind, Cold, and Dampness invade the wrist channels, they cause the tissues to tighten and fluids to stagnate. This constriction and swelling compress the median nerve, leading to the characteristic pain, numbness, and tingling that feel worse in cold or damp weather and improve with warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, slightly swollen with teeth marks and a white greasy coating (苔白腻, tái bái nì). Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and tight (紧 jǐn), or slow (迟 chí).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind, Cold, and Dampness are pathogenic factors that constrict the channels and obstruct the flow of Qi and Blood in the wrist. Warmth relaxes the tissues and promotes circulation, while gentle movement prevents stagnation without aggravating inflammation. Cold and damp environments reinforce the pathogenic factors, worsening the obstruction and pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep your wrist warm with a brace or sleeve, especially in cold or damp weather. Apply a warm compress or soak the hand in warm ginger water to improve circulation. Gentle stretching and range-of-motion exercises can prevent stiffness, but avoid heavy gripping or repetitive strain. Eat warm, cooked foods and avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that promote internal Dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and Blood remain stagnant in the wrist for a long time, fluids can thicken into a sticky obstruction called Phlegm. This Phlegm lodges in the narrow carpal tunnel, blocking the meridians that run through the wrist. The result is a heavy, swollen sensation, deep aching pain, and a dulled, clumsy feeling in the hand that doesn't change much with rest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple body with stasis spots, white greasy coating, distended sublingual veins. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), or wiry and slippery (滑 huá) if Phlegm predominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm is a congealed form of Dampness that thickens in cold, stagnant conditions. Warmth and movement help transform and disperse it, while cold and dampness encourage it to settle and harden. Greasy foods add to the body's Dampness load, directly feeding the Phlegm that blocks the wrist.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Reduce greasy, fried, and dairy-heavy foods that encourage Phlegm. Eat lightly cooked vegetables, moderate amounts of warming spices like ginger, and drink warm fluids. Gentle daily wrist stretches and whole-body movement help keep Qi and fluids moving rather than stagnating.

patterns.pattern_name: Painful Obstruction due to Damp Heat in Channels
patterns.symptoms: ["Red, swollen wrist that feels hot to the touch", "Burning pain in the wrist and hand", "Pain relieved by cold, worsened by warmth", "Heavy, aching sensation in the forearm", "Thirst and feeling of bodily heat", "Pain worse at night"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot, humid weather, Greasy, spicy, or fried foods, Heat packs or warm soaks, Repetitive wrist movements, Alcohol
patterns.better_with: Cold compress on the wrist, Resting the hand, Cool, dry weather, Light, non-greasy meals
patterns.why_this_happens: When repetitive friction or local inflammation generates heat and dampness inside the wrist, these two pathogens combine and lodge in the carpal tunnel. Dampness makes tissues swell and feel heavy, while heat creates redness and a burning sensation. Together they compress the median nerve, producing the characteristic hot, swollen, and painful wrist that feels worse with warmth and better with cold.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy (sticky) coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid (滑数, huá shuò), sometimes soggy or wiry at the middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is a combination of two pathogenic factors: Dampness, which is heavy, sticky, and causes swelling, and Heat, which causes redness and burning pain. Heat and humidity from the environment or from greasy, spicy foods add more Damp-Heat to the body, making the wrist feel worse. Cold compresses and cooling foods directly counteract the Heat component, while rest prevents further friction and inflammation from building up. Drying, cooling herbs and acupuncture points that drain Dampness and clear Heat address both pathogens at once, shrinking the swollen tissues and relieving the burning sensation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods that generate internal Dampness and Heat. Eat more cooling, moisture-draining foods like cucumber, celery, mung beans, and barley. Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth to the wrist for 10-15 minutes when burning pain flares, and rest the hand during acute episodes.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and Blood are chronically deficient, the channels and sinews that run through the wrist are not properly nourished. This leads to a dull, persistent numbness and tingling in the hand, along with weakness and a tendency for symptoms to worsen with fatigue or overuse. Unlike patterns driven by acute stagnation or cold, the discomfort here is more a sense of emptiness and lack of strength.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: Fine (thin) and weak, especially in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are the body's nourishment. Overwork, cold, and poor diet deplete them further, causing the wrist channels to become malnourished and numb. Rest, warmth, and nourishing foods replenish Qi and Blood, while gentle movement encourages circulation without straining the already weak constitution.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like bone broths, stews, dark leafy greens, and small amounts of red meat or liver. Avoid cold, raw foods and irregular meals that weaken the Spleen. Gentle exercises such as Tai Chi or Qi Gong build Qi without depleting it, and regular rest for the wrist is essential.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork and prolonged computer use, Spicy, fried, or heating foods, Late nights and insufficient sleep, Emotional stress and frustration, Dry, heated indoor environments
patterns.better_with: Resting the wrist and hand, Cool or room-temperature compress, Moistening, Yin-nourishing foods, Consistent, early bedtime, Gentle, non-repetitive movement
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney and Liver Yin is the deep foundation that moistens and nourishes the sinews and joints. When it becomes depleted, the tendons and ligaments in the wrist lose their natural lubrication and resilience, becoming dry, tight, and prone to dysfunction even under ordinary use. The deficiency heat that arises from the Yin void can create a subtle burning or warm sensation in the wrist, and because Yin is meant to anchor Yang at night, the numbness and discomfort often worsen in the evening or during sleep.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, and a dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, and wiry; the left Chi (Kidney) position is weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Liver Yin is easily consumed by overwork, late nights, and heating foods, which is exactly what worsens this pattern. Rest, sleep, and moistening foods allow Yin to regenerate, cooling the deficiency heat and re-lubricating the sinews. Gentle movement encourages local Blood flow without spending Yin, while cold compresses directly soothe the warm, dry sensation in the wrist.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize deep rest and a consistent sleep schedule, as Yin rebuilds itself at night. Eat plenty of moistening, Yin-nourishing foods like black sesame, walnuts, goji berries, yam, and lightly cooked greens. Strictly avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods, and limit coffee and alcohol, which deplete Yin. Gentle wrist stretches can help, but avoid repetitive strain until the deep Yin is restored.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help carpal tunnel syndrome?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture is one of the most researched complementary therapies for carpal tunnel syndrome. It works by releasing local muscle tension, improving blood flow through the wrist, and reducing inflammation around the median nerve. In TCM terms, it opens the blocked meridians and moves stagnant Qi and Blood. Many patients experience reduced numbness and pain after just a few sessions, especially when acupuncture is combined with herbal medicine and lifestyle adjustments.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture treatments will I need?
faqs.answer: The number of sessions depends on your pattern and how long you’ve had symptoms. For excess patterns like Qi and Blood Stagnation or Wind-Cold-Damp, noticeable improvement often occurs within 4-6 weekly sessions. Deficiency patterns, where the body needs to rebuild Qi and Blood or Yin, typically require 8-12 sessions or more. Your practitioner will reassess your progress regularly and adjust the frequency as symptoms improve. Many patients continue with maintenance treatments every few weeks to prevent recurrence.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with my wrist splint or other conventional treatments?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM works well alongside conventional approaches. You can continue wearing a wrist splint, especially at night, while receiving acupuncture and taking herbs. If you are using NSAIDs or have had corticosteroid injections, inform your practitioner, as some herbs that move Blood (such as Dang Gui and Chuan Xiong) may have mild blood-thinning effects. Always bring a list of your medications and supplements to your TCM consultation so your practitioner can ensure there are no interactions.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Dietary adjustments can support your recovery, but they don’t have to be drastic. Generally, avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which constrict the channels and may worsen pain. Favour warm, cooked meals and incorporate circulation-boosting spices like ginger, turmeric, and cinnamon. If your symptoms feel worse in cold or damp weather, add warming foods like black pepper and cloves. If you have heat signs (redness, burning), steer clear of spicy, greasy, and fried foods. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe if I’m considering surgery?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many patients use TCM to manage symptoms while deciding about surgery, or to prepare for and recover from an operation. Acupuncture and herbs can reduce inflammation and pain pre-operatively, and may speed healing afterwards. However, you must inform both your surgeon and your TCM practitioner about all treatments you are receiving. If you are taking herbs that affect blood clotting, your surgeon may ask you to pause them before the procedure. Never stop prescribed medications without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture in the wrist hurt?
faqs.answer: Most people find acupuncture on the wrist to be very tolerable. The needles used are extremely thin - much finer than a typical injection needle. You may feel a brief pinch as the needle is inserted, followed by a mild ache, warmth, or tingling sensation that signals the arrival of Qi. Many patients actually find the experience relaxing and report that local needling brings immediate relief of the heavy, numb sensation in their hand.

faqs.question: Can TCM prevent carpal tunnel from coming back?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance that made you susceptible in the first place, which can significantly reduce the risk of recurrence. For example, if your problem stemmed from Qi and Blood Stagnation due to repetitive strain, treatment will not only clear the current blockage but also strengthen the channels and teach you stretches and ergonomic habits. If deficiency was the root, building Qi and Blood or nourishing Yin provides lasting resilience. Many patients find that periodic “tune-up” treatments and mindful self-care keep symptoms from returning.

research.title: Acupuncture in treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: A randomized controlled trial study
research.description: This RCT compared acupuncture with sham acupuncture and found that real acupuncture significantly reduced pain, numbness, and functional impairment in patients with mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome. The improvements were maintained at follow-up.
research.periodical: Khosrawi S, et al. (2012). Acupuncture in treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: A randomized controlled trial study. Journal of Research in Medical Sciences, 17(1), 1-7.

research.title: Efficacy of acupuncture and night splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized clinical trial
research.description: This trial compared acupuncture, night splinting, and their combination. Acupuncture alone and in combination with splinting provided greater relief of symptoms and improvement in nerve conduction than splinting alone, supporting acupuncture as an effective standalone treatment.
research.periodical: Kumnerddee W, et al. (2010). Efficacy of acupuncture and night splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized clinical trial. Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand, 93(12), 1463-1469.

research.title: The effectiveness of acupuncture in the treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: Patients receiving acupuncture showed significant improvements in symptom severity and functional status scores compared to a control group. The study concluded that acupuncture is a safe and effective conservative treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome.
research.periodical: Yao E, et al. (2012). The effectiveness of acupuncture in the treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine, 18(5), 487-492.
